title: Transactional Writing Foundations Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the main transactional writing forms and what makes each tick.
meta_desc: GCSE English Language transactional writing walkthrough — letters, articles, speeches and leaflets.
final_note: You learned the key forms of transactional writing and the basics of register and audience.

concepts.def: Letter (Dear Sir/Madam), article (headline, byline), speech (direct address), report; conventions matter.

walkthroughs.body_html: A letter needs address and sign-off. An article needs a headline. Match the conventions.

Writing to your headteacher? Formal: full sentences, no contractions, 'Yours sincerely'.

Writing to a friend? Informal: contractions, slang, 'See ya'.
Teenagers want energy and humour. Local councillors want clarity and respect. Adjust vocabulary, examples and references to match.

mcqs.q: Why do text types like letters and articles have predictable features?
options: Because their conventions, such as a headline or sign-off, help readers recognise the form and purpose.
Because every text type uses identical features.
Because writers must rigidly copy a template for no real reason.
The form is chosen only by counting the words required.

mcqs.q: How should the form of a transactional text be chosen?
options: Any form works equally well for any task.
The form is chosen only by counting the words required.
A counter-argument means writing the whole piece twice.
To match the purpose and audience, e.g. a formal letter to complain or a leaflet to inform.

mcqs.q: What is the role of a counter-argument in persuasive writing?
options: Because every text type uses identical features.
A counter-argument weakens your writing and should be avoided.
A counter-argument means writing the whole piece twice.
To acknowledge an opposing view and then refute it, strengthening your own case.
